blocks.text: Specialized Treatment for College Students

Living with a drug or alcohol addiction can bring unwanted chaos into your life. You can distance yourself from loved ones and friends, develop new or worsening mental health and physical health concerns, and find yourself with financial difficulties.

For college students who struggle with drug or alcohol misuse and abuse, there are a unique set of experiences and challenges that can impact their experience. Drug and alcohol use is widely accepted for college students, and even expected. This reality can make it difficult for loved ones to pick up on a college students’ use. Additionally, they are in an environment often with easy access to a variety of substances.

Substance Abuse Rates Among College Students
A 2018 report published by the National Institute on Drug Abuse compared substance use rates of college students ages 19-22 to other individuals within the same age range who are not students.

A key finding, which has been supported by other research, is that binge drinking is a significant concern for college students. This study showed that 28% of college students participated in binge drinking within the two weeks prior to taking the survey. This was the first time that this rate has been found below 30%.

Binge drinking occurs when an individual drinks five or more drinks in a row. This form of drinking increases an individual’s risk of injury and their risk of alcohol-related concerns, such as alcohol poisoning.

Why Do College Students Use Drugs?

There are many reasons why college students use drugs and drink alcohol. As mentioned above, experimentation with drugs and alcohol is often expected of college students, which can make it feel like a “normal” part of the college experience. Peer pressure may contribute to this as well.

College students often have access to a variety of substances on a college campus which can create an environment where using is easier. For some students, college is their first time without supervision or guidance of older adults, so they are trying to find their own boundaries when it comes to drug and alcohol use.
Some students are curious about what it is like to use drugs and alcohol. This can be particularly true for students who did not try alcohol or drugs before attending college.

Which Drugs Are Most Common in College?

According to the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), the most commonly abused substance on college campuses is alcohol. This should not be too surprising given the significant presence of binge drinking on campuses. Alcohol is followed by marijuana, hallucinogens, prescription pain relievers, cocaine, stimulants, inhalants, meth, and heroin, respectively.

What Are the Signs a College Student is Abusing Drugs?

It is important to note that some of the signs and symptoms associated with drug and alcohol abuse in a college student could be indicative of other mental health concerns, including depression and anxiety. Because of this, we encourage you to be compassionate and patient when talking to your loved one about your concerns.
Signs and symptoms associated with drug and alcohol abuse for college students include:
Drop in grades
Unexplained absenteeism
Appearing impaired often
Dishonesty, lying, manipulation
Changes to eating and sleeping patterns
Change in grooming
Change in friend group
New or worsening legal concerns
Moodiness and irritability
Needing to drink or use to avoid being sick

What Are the Challenges in College Student Addiction Treatment

If a college student is struggling with drugs or alcohol, it is imperative that they receive the help they deserve. The presence of drugs and alcohol on college campuses can contribute to relapses and serve as challenging triggers for individuals in recovery.

College can be a stressful time in a person’s life. Trying to excel in school, while in the early stages of recovery is hard! Addiction treatment can provide students with an invaluable source of support and encouragement. Additionally, college student rehabs can help them connect with other students who have relatable experiences.
